title: Silicon-Germanium Heterostructures with Enhanced Valley Splitting for Spin Qubits
authors: David W. Kanaar, Efrain Martinez, Peihong Zhang, Mark F. Gyure
abstract: Achieving valley splittings well in excess of the thermal energy of electrons and avoiding valley excitations is essential for the consistent initialization, operation and readout of gate-defined Si spin qubits. In this work, we present a device-level optimization strategy for pushing valley splittings to between 1 and 5 meV, well beyond values reported in nearly all previous theoretical studies. Using device-scale simulations that incorporate atomistic alloy disorder through a 1D tight-binding theory, we demonstrate that our proposed approach yields large valley splittings with a tight distribution across disorder realizations, a key requirement for reproducible qubit performance at scale. The approach rests on an unorthodox Si/SiGe heterostructure design combining a narrow quantum well, a small Ge spike, and a pure-Ge cap. We corroborate these predictions with targeted atomistic density functional theory calculations. These results offer a clear path forward for scalable Si/SiGe spin qubit devices and, if realized experimentally, effectively eliminate valley splitting as an existential problem for large scale SiGe-based quantum processors.
summary: The paper proposes an advanced $	ext{Si}/	ext{SiGe}$ heterostructure design—combining a narrow well, pure-Ge cap, and Ge spike—to drastically enhance valley splitting in spin qubit platforms. Using detailed simulations, the authors demonstrate that this engineered structure can achieve splittings up to $5 	ext{ meV}$, effectively mitigating valley splitting as an obstacle for scalable quantum processors.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving valley splittings significantly larger than thermal energy ($k_B T$) in Si/SiGe heterostructures to ensure reliable initialization, operation, and readout of spin qubits.
main_result: An unorthodox design combining a narrow quantum well, a pure-Ge cap, and a dilute Ge spike can push valley splittings up to $\sim 5 	ext{ meV}$ with low variance across disorder realizations.
method: The work uses device-scale simulations incorporating atomistic alloy disorder via 1D tight-binding theory, corroborated by targeted DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The system is gate-defined Si/SiGe heterostructures designed for spin qubits. The model involves engineering the Ge concentration profile ($\chi(z)$) through a specific three-part structure: narrow quantum well, pure-Ge cap, and dilute Ge spike.
key_observables: Valley splitting ($\Delta E_v$), which must be significantly larger than $k_B T$ (i.e., $> 1 	ext{ meV}$ for reliable operation).
important_parameters: Well width ($W_w$, e.g., $2.5-3.0 	ext{ nm}$), pure-Ge cap thickness ($	ext{NML}=1$), and dilute Ge spike concentration ($f_{	ext{Ge}} \approx 4\%$). Interface sharpness ($\sigma$) is critical.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes atomically sharp interfaces to establish an upper bound, though it quantifies the required interface sharpness (e.g., $\sigma_{cap} \approx 1-2 	ext{ ML}$) needed for $E_v \gtrsim 1 	ext{ meV}$ in realistic scenarios.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how valley splitting varies with well width, cap thickness, and spike concentration, demonstrating the additive enhancement from the proposed three-component structure. Later figures quantify the dependence on interface broadening ($\sigma_{cap}, \sigma_{spike}$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical requirement for large valley splittings, proposes an unorthodox $	ext{Si}/	ext{SiGe}$ design (narrow well + pure-Ge cap + Ge spike), and uses 1D tight-binding/DFT simulations to show that this combination yields high, reproducible splitting values. It then analyzes how interface broadening degrades this performance.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical material science bottleneck for solid-state quantum computing by providing an engineering blueprint (heterostructure design) to overcome fundamental energy level limitations in silicon qubits.
